To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) when the rape is defined as intergroup violence (i.e., “hate crime”) instead of interpersonal violence (i.e. “personal assault”), participants blame the perpetrator more and the victim less, and (2) when the perpetrator is an acquaintance, participants blame the victim more and the perpetrator less.

defining rape as an intergroup crime, as compared to defining it as an act of personal violence, led to less victim blaming, and participants blamed victims more when they were attacked by an acquaintance than by a stranger.
